'''Robert Gayle Roeder''' (born June 3, 1942, in [[Boonville, Indiana|Boonville]], Indiana, United States) is an American biochemist. He is known as a pioneer scientist in [[eukaryotic transcription]]. He discovered three distinct nuclear [[RNA polymerases]] in 1969<ref name="pmid5344598"/> and characterized many proteins involved in the regulation of transcription, including basic [[transcription factors]] and the first mammalian gene-specific [[Activator (genetics)|activator]] over five decades of research.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Roeder RG | title = 50+ years of eukaryotic transcription: an expanding universe of factors and mechanisms | journal =  Nature Structural & Molecular Biology | volume = 26 | issue = 9 | pages = 783–791 |date=Sep 2019 | pmid = 31439941 | doi =10.1038/s41594-019-0287-x | pmc = 6867066 }}</ref> He is the recipient of the [[Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize]] in 1999,the [[Gairdner Foundation International Award]] in 2000, the [[Albert Lasker Award for Basic Medical Research]] in 2003, and the [[Kyoto Prize]] in 2021. He currently serves as [[Arnold and Mabel Beckman]] Professor and Head of the Laboratory of Biochemical and Molecular Biology at [[Rockefeller University]].

==Biography==

Roeder was born in Boonville, Indiana, US in 1942. He received his B.A. ''summa cum laude'' in chemistry from [[Wabash College]] in 1964 and his M.S. in chemistry from the [[University of Illinois]] in 1965. He received his Ph.D. in biochemistry in 1969 from the [[University of Washington]], Seattle, where he worked with [[William J. Rutter]]. He did postdoctoral work with [[Donald D. Brown]] at the [[Carnegie Institution of Washington]], in Baltimore, from 1969 to 1971. He was a member of the faculty at [[Washington University School of Medicine]] in St. Louis from 1971 to 1982, when he joined [[Rockefeller University]]. In 1985, he was named Arnold and Mabel Beckman Professor. He was elected as a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] in 1988 and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1995, and a foreign associate member of the [[European Molecular Biology Organization]] in 2003.

==Major scientific discoveries==

* 1969: As a graduate student at the University of Washington, Roeder discovers that three enzymes, called [[RNA polymerase]]s, directly copy [[DNA]] to [[RNA]] in eukaryotic organisms ranging from yeast to mammals.<ref name="pmid5344598">{{cite journal |vauthors=Roeder RG, Rutter WJ | title = Multiple forms of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase in eukaryotic organisms | journal = Nature | volume = 224 | issue = 5216 | pages = 234–7 |date=Oct 1969 | pmid = 5344598 | doi =10.1038/224234a0 | bibcode = 1969Natur.224..234R | s2cid = 4283528 }}</ref>
* 1971–1977: As a professor at Washington University in St. Louis, he goes on to show that these enzymes, referred to as Pol I, II and III, have complex subunit structures with both distinct and common polypeptides, recognize and copy distinct classes of genes, respectively, of large ribosomal RNAs, mRNA precursors, and transfer and 5S RNAs.<ref name="pmid1054509">{{cite journal |vauthors=Sklar VE, Schwartz LB, Roeder RG | title = Distinct molecular structures of nuclear class I, II and III DNA-dependent RNA polymerases | journal = Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A | volume = 72 | issue = 1  | pages = 348–52 |date=Jan 1975 | pmid = 1054509 | doi =10.1073/pnas.72.1.348 | pmc = 432302 | bibcode = 1975PNAS...72..348S | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="pmid4558099">{{cite journal |vauthors=Reeder RH, Roeder RG | title = Ribosomal RNA synthesis in isolated nuclei | journal = J Mol Biol | volume = 67 | issue = 3  | pages = 433–41 |date=Jun 1972 | pmid = 4558099 | doi =10.1016/0022-2836(72)90461-5 }}</ref><ref name="pmid4525293">{{cite journal |vauthors=Weinmann R, Roeder RG | title = Role of DNA-Dependent RNA Polymerase III in the Transcription of the tRNA and 5S RNA Genes | journal = Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A | volume = 71 | issue = 5  | pages = 1790–4 |date=May 1974 | pmid = 4525293 | pmc =  388326| doi =10.1073/pnas.71.5.1790 | bibcode = 1974PNAS...71.1790W | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="pmid4530313">{{cite journal |vauthors=Weinmann R, Raskas HJ, Roeder RG | title = Role of DNA-Dependent RNA Polymerases II and III in Transcription of the Adenovirus Genome Late in Productive Infection | journal = Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A | volume = 71 | issue = 9  | pages = 3426–39 |date=Sep 1974 | pmid = 4530313 | pmc =  433786| doi =10.1073/pnas.71.9.3426 | bibcode = 1974PNAS...71.3426W | doi-access = free }}</ref>
* 1977–1979: Roeder develops cell-free systems to better study [[Transcription (biology)|transcription]].<ref name="pmid264693">{{cite journal |vauthors=Parker CS, Roeder RG | title = Selective and accurate transcription of the Xenopus laevis 5S RNA genes in isolated chromatin by purified RNA polymerase III | journal = Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A | volume = 74 | issue = 1  | pages = 44–8 |date=Jan 1977 | pmid = 264693 | pmc =  393193| doi =10.1073/pnas.74.1.44 | bibcode = 1977PNAS...74...44P | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="pmid284325">{{cite journal |vauthors=Ng SY, Parker CS, Roeder RG | title = Transcription of cloned Xenopus 5S RNA genes by X. laevis RNA polymerase III in reconstituted systems | journal = Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A | volume =  76 | issue = 1  | pages = 136–40 |date=Jan 1979 | pmid = 284325 | pmc =  382891| doi =10.1073/pnas.76.1.136 | bibcode = 1979PNAS...76..136N | doi-access = free }}</ref> Composed of the purified RNA polymerases and components extracted from cell nuclei, the systems allow researchers to recreate transcription in a test tube in a way that faithfully mimics the real process in cells.<ref name="pmid498279">{{cite journal |vauthors=Weil PA, Luse DS, Segall J, Roeder RG | title = Selective and accurate initiation of transcription at the Ad2 major late promotor in a soluble system dependent on purified RNA polymerase II and DNA | journal = Cell | volume = 18 | issue = 2  | pages = 469–84 |date=Oct 1979 | pmid = 498279 | doi =10.1016/0092-8674(79)90065-5 | s2cid = 34095322 }}</ref><ref name="pmid277365">{{cite journal |vauthors=Parker CS, Jaehning JA, Roeder RG | title = Faithful gene transcription by eukaryotic RNA polymerases in reconstructed systems  | journal =  Cold Spring Harb Symp Quant Biol | volume = 42 | issue = 1  | pages = 577–87 |date= 1978 | pmid = 277365 | doi =10.1101/sqb.1978.042.01.060}}</ref>
* 1979–1980: The development of cell-free systems leads to the identification of complex sets of proteins called accessory factors that are essential for each individual RNA polymerase (e.g., [[TFIIA]], [[TFIIB]], [[TFIIE]], [[TFIIF]] and [[TFIIH]] for Pol II, and TFIIIB and TFIIIC for Pol III) to "read" specific target genes.<ref name="pmid7440579">{{cite journal |vauthors=Segall J, Matsui T, Roeder RG | title = Multiple factors are required for the accurate transcription of purified genes by RNA polymerase III | journal = J Biol Chem | volume = 255 | issue = 24  | pages = 11986–91 |date=Dec 1980 | doi = 10.1016/S0021-9258(19)70231-2 | pmid = 7440579 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="pmid7440580">{{cite journal |vauthors=Matsui T, Segall J, Weil PA, Roeder RG | title = Multiple factors required for accurate initiation of transcription by purified RNA polymerase II | journal = J Biol Chem | volume = 255 | issue = 24  | pages = 11992–6 |date=Dec 1980 | doi = 10.1016/S0021-9258(19)70232-4 | pmid = 7440580 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Roeder RG, Engelke DR, Luse DS, Segall J, Shastry BS, Weil PA | title = Factors involved in the transcription of purified genes by RNA polymerase III | journal = ICN-UCLA Symposium on Gene Regulation in Eukaryote | volume=eds. R. Axel and T. Maniatis. Academic Press, New York  | pages = 521–540 |date=1979 }}</ref>
* 1980: Roeder identifies the first mammalian gene-specific activator, called [[TFIIIA]].<ref name="pmid6153931">{{cite journal |vauthors=Engelke DR, Ng SY, Shastry BS, Roeder RG | title = Specific interaction of a purified transcription factor with an internal control region of 5S RNA genes | journal = Cell | volume = 19 | issue = 3  | pages = 717–28 |date=Mar 1980 | pmid = 6153931 | doi =10.1016/S0092-8674(80)80048-1 | s2cid = 23955175 }}</ref> TFIIIA and similar proteins bind to specific DNA sequences and enhance the reading of corresponding target genes. Repressors perform the opposite task by inhibiting a gene's activity.
* 1990s: A decade of research culminates with the discovery of [[coactivator]]s, large protein complexes that provide a bridge between the [[Activator (genetics)|activator]]s and [[repressor]]s and the [[RNA polymerases]] and other components of the general [[Transcription (biology)|transcription]] machinery.<ref name="pmid1889091">{{cite journal |vauthors=Meisterernst M, Roy AL, Lieu HM, Roeder RG | title = Activation of class II gene transcription by regulatory factors is potentiated by a novel activity | journal = Cell | volume = 66 | issue = 5  | pages = 981–93 |date=Sep 1991 | pmid = 1889091 | doi =10.1016/0092-8674(91)90443-3 | s2cid = 43608887 }}</ref><ref name="pmid8062391">{{cite journal |vauthors=Ge H, Roeder RG | title = Purification, cloning, and characterization of a human coactivator, PC4, that mediates transcriptional activation of class II genes | journal = Cell | volume = 78 | issue = 3  | pages = 513–23 |date=Aug 1994 | pmid = 8062391 | doi =10.1016/0092-8674(94)90428-6 | s2cid = 1140379 }}</ref>
*1992: Roeder laboratory demonstrates that [[coactivator]]s can be ubiquitous, monitoring many genes in a variety of cells, or specific to one particular cell type. Roeder and colleagues introduce the concept of cell specificity after they demonstrate that the coactivator OCA-B, the first cell-specific coactivator, discovered by Roeder in 1992, is unique to immune system B cells.<ref name="pmid1423591">{{cite journal |vauthors=Luo Y, Fujii H, Gerster T, Roeder RG | title = A novel B cell-derived coactivator potentiates the activation of immunoglobulin promoters by octamer-binding transcription factors | journal = Cell | volume = 71 | issue = 2  | pages = 231–41 |date=Oct 1992 | pmid = 1423591 | doi =10.1016/0092-8674(92)90352-D | s2cid = 24583386 }}</ref>
*1996: Roeder's laboratory discovers the major conduit for communication between gene-specific activators and the general transcription machinery in animal cells: a giant coactivator (TRAP/SMCC) that consists of about 25 different protein chains and is referred to as the human [[Mediator (coactivator)|mediator]] after its counterpart in yeast.<ref name="pmid8710870">{{cite journal |vauthors=Fondell JD, Ge H, Roeder RG | title = Ligand induction of a transcriptionally active thyroid hormone receptor coactivator complex | journal = Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A | volume = 93 | issue = 16  | pages = 8329–33 |date=Aug 1996 | pmid = 8710870 | pmc =  38670| doi =10.1073/pnas.93.16.8329 | bibcode = 1996PNAS...93.8329F | doi-access = free }}</ref>
*2002: Roeder and colleagues show that a single component of the [[Mediator (coactivator)|mediator]] is essential for the formation of fat cells — a finding that may one day contribute to new treatments for diabetes, heart disease, cancer and other conditions in which the fat-making process breaks down.<ref name="pmid12037571">{{cite journal |vauthors=Ge K, Guermah M, Yuan CX, Ito M, Wallberg AE, Spiegelman BM, Roeder RG | title = Transcription coactivator TRAP220 is required for PPAR gamma 2-stimulated adipogenesis | journal = Nature | volume = 417 | issue = 6888  | pages = 563–7 |date=May 2002 | pmid = 12037571 | doi =10.1038/417563a | bibcode = 2002Natur.417..563G | s2cid = 4432077 }}</ref>

==Prominent alumni of the Roeder Laboratory==
The Roeder Laboratory has trained hundreds of students and postdoctoral fellows, many of whom hold independent positions in prominent biomedical research institutions, including Richard A. Bernstein ([[Northwestern University]]),  [[Robert B. Darnell]] ([[Rockefeller University]] and [[HHMI]]), Beverly M. Emerson ([[Salk Institute for Biological Studies]]), Michael R. Green ([[University of Massachusetts Medical School]] and [[HHMI]]), Wei Gu ([[Columbia University]]), Nathaniel Heintz ([[Rockefeller University]] and [[HHMI]]), Andrew B. Lassar ([[Harvard Medical School]]), Carl S. Parker ([[California Institute of Technology]]), Ron Prywes ([[Columbia University]]), Danny Reinberg ([[New York University School of Medicine]] and [[HHMI]]), Hazel L. Sive ([[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] and [[Whitehead Institute]]) and Jerry Workman ([[Stowers Institute for Medical Research]]).<ref name="pmid14636549">{{cite journal |vauthors=Abmayr SM, Workman JL | title = Transcription factors prominently in Lasker Award to Roeder | journal = Cell | volume = 115 | issue = 3 | pages = 243–6 |date=Oct 2003 | pmid = 14636549 | doi =10.1016/S0092-8674(03)00846-8 | s2cid = 17097436 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
